metadata.title: GEEK Protocol — Kaspa conventions follow-up
metadata.schema: correctIndex is zero-based; options contains four distinct strings
metadata.reviewNotice: Internally source-checked original questions about the cited KCC document snapshot. Normative convention requirements are not claims of universal wallet support, finalization, migration approval or current network acceptance. Difficulty is provisional.
metadata.attribution: GEEK Protocol original questions; Kaspanet KCC documents are CC0 primary evidence. No source prose or code is imported.

questions.prompt: Under the KCC-0 guidelines, what kind of proposal belongs in a KIP rather than a KCC?
options: A change to Kaspa consensus or core-node behavior
A shared wallet discovery convention
A common application interface layout for wallet integrations
An ecosystem token interoperability convention
questions.funFact: KCCs coordinate ecosystem conventions; KCC-0 directs consensus and core-node changes to KIPs.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Under KCC-0, what does a convention becoming Final mean for a wallet developer?
options: It automatically updates every installed wallet
It marks ecosystem convergence without forcing that wallet to implement it
It proves every wallet already supports the convention
It requires the wallet to use one particular vendor
questions.funFact: Final status describes the convention. Each participant still decides whether to implement it.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: In the KCC-0 lifecycle, what is the purpose of Last Call?
options: A deadline for users to sell a token
A signal that all wallet deployments are complete
A final review window before a proposal can move to Final
A request to stop accepting network transactions
questions.funFact: Last Call is a standards review stage, not a trading instruction or deployment certificate.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: What do conformance vectors provide for a Kaspa convention that defines byte layouts or hashes?
options: A list of validators allowed to change consensus
A guarantee that a wallet has no security bugs
A replacement for the convention specification
Concrete test cases for comparing an implementation with the specified results
questions.funFact: KCC-0 requires human-readable and machine-readable vectors for the relevant Standards Track conventions. Passing them does not certify every application behavior.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Under KCC-0, how should a substantive change to a Final convention be made, apart from its stated defect-correction process?
options: Through a new KCC that supersedes the old convention
By silently replacing the old specification text
By treating a wallet release note as the new standard
By letting each implementation redefine existing fields locally
questions.funFact: KCC-0 distinguishes limited corrections and clarifications from other substantive changes, which require an explicit superseding KCC.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Why does the KCC-20 convention require a token program artifact?
options: To publish every holder's balance on L1
To describe how clients decode token state and construct transfers
To register the token with a central KCC registry
To replace transaction validation with off-chain indexing
questions.funFact: The artifact exposes the program ABI and token configuration needed by compatible readers and transaction builders.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Within one KCC-20 covenant family, when does the KCC specification's standard treat states as fungible with one another?
options: Whenever their displayed tickers are identical
Whenever their KAS carrier values are identical
When their extension commitments are identical
Whenever their owners use the same wallet app
questions.funFact: The standard treats extended state as opaque but includes its commitment in token identity for fungibility. A standard transfer preserves that shared commitment.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Why must a KCC-20 transfer reject a successor owner scheme that the token configuration does not support?
options: Different owner schemes always change the token's decimals
Every recipient must reuse the sender's original owner scheme and key
Owner schemes determine the Kaspa block production rate
The resulting token state could otherwise become unspendable
questions.funFact: KCC-20 requires validation of successor owner schemes so a transfer cannot create a state whose authorization method the token cannot handle.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: What does KCC-20 borrowed receive let a sender do under the recipient state's borrowing policy?
options: Add tokens to an existing recipient state without that recipient authorizing the transaction
Spend tokens out of the recipient's state without restrictions
Take ownership of every state held by the recipient
Receive a loan that must later be repaid with interest
questions.funFact: Borrowed receive reuses and recreates a recipient UTXO with more tokens. It does not transfer its ownership to the sender or create a lending debt.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: What happens to the KAS value carried by the recipient state during a valid KCC-20 borrowed receive?
options: The sender may use all of it for unrelated fees
Its successor must carry at least as much KAS as the borrowed input
It must always become exactly zero
It is automatically converted into token units
questions.funFact: The borrowed-receive rules protect the recipient's existing KAS carrier value while adding token quantity.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Under the KCC-20 amount-threshold borrow scheme, the effective threshold is 10 base units. Which increase satisfies the amount rule?
options: An increase of exactly 10 base units
An increase of 9 base units
An increase of 11 base units
An unchanged token amount
questions.funFact: The increase must be strictly greater than the effective threshold. This checks the amount condition only; the transaction must still satisfy every other rule.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Which KCC-20 path may choose new borrowing settings for its output states?
options: A borrowed receive that changes settings without owner approval
An explorer changing its local token label
A sender merely knowing the recipient address
A normal owner-authorized transfer
questions.funFact: The owner-authorized path may set new borrow policies. Borrowed receive must preserve the borrow scheme and follow the scheme's guard-update rule.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: In the KCC-20 multi-input transfer convention, how do leader and delegator checks differ?
options: The leader checks the complete transition; each delegator authenticates its local owner
Delegators may create extra token quantity independently
Only the last output checks every input owner
The leader skips successor validation once a delegator signs
questions.funFact: Delegators authorize their own inputs while the leader validates conservation and all successor states for the shared transition.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: How must an implementation treat an unassigned KCC-20 borrow-scheme value under the KCC specification's convention?
options: Interpret it as unrestricted borrowing by default
Reject it as invalid rather than invent a local meaning
Treat it as the most recently supported scheme in the token family
Accept it whenever the transaction fee is high enough
questions.funFact: Unassigned borrow-scheme selectors are reserved for future KCCs. Guessing their meaning would break interoperability and authorization checks.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: For KCC-2 covenant-ID authority, what is the minimum transaction participation requirement?
options: A transaction output may merely display the same token ticker
A website must list the authority in its page title
A spent input must belong to the identified covenant lineage
The transaction must use an address with the longest text
questions.funFact: The minimum check uses a consensus-authenticated input from the specified lineage. Applications can require additional program, state and transition checks.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: When checking a KCC-2 P2SH authority, why is matching only a program template insufficient?
options: The authority ignores script contents whenever a fee is paid
Every template always belongs to the same private key
The authority is identified only by its human-readable name
The authority commits to the exact redeem script, including its embedded state
questions.funFact: A P2SH authority commits to every byte of its redeem script. Similar structure does not establish the required exact-script authority.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Why can the presence of a matching KCC-2 authority input still be insufficient to prove approval of an application's intended action?
options: A permissive authority program may allow participation without constraining that action
A matching authority input always invalidates the transaction
Transaction fees replace the application's authorization policy
The input owner automatically approves every future application action
questions.funFact: Applications must ensure the authority's rules constrain its participation or add suitable template, state and transition checks.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: In the KCC-23 metadata convention, where is the JSON declaration placed before covenant genesis?
options: In every future token transfer's recipient signature
In the payload of a preparation transaction whose output genesis spends
Only in an off-chain JSON file hosted by the issuer
In the coinbase payload of the block mining the genesis
questions.funFact: The preparation transaction commits to the JSON bytes. Genesis spends its output to bind that declaration to the covenant identity.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Under KCC-23, which metadata representation does the covenant binding commit to?
options: Only the token name with all other fields ignored
Any JSON text that parses to the same object
The exact payload bytes, including codec prefix, whitespace and property order
A freely editable description kept only by one explorer
questions.funFact: Equivalent-looking JSON serializations can have different bytes. KCC-23 binds the exact declaration, fixed for that covenant ID.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.

questions.prompt: Does declaring metadata through KCC-23 itself grant a new right to spend the covenant's tokens?
options: Yes; the declarer becomes the token's mint authority
Yes; any explorer may then spend a holder's balance
Yes; changing a displayed name replaces the token's signatures
No; it binds descriptive metadata without changing spending authority
questions.funFact: KCC-23 binds descriptive information. The covenant's actual validation rules continue to determine spending authorization.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question; Kaspanet KCC documents provide primary evidence, not endorsement.
